top.title: An anti-aging drug may help protect the brain before Alzheimer's symptoms begin
top.summary: A surprising new study suggests that an anti-aging drug could help protect people genetically predisposed to Alzheimer's disease. Researchers found that just four weeks of low-dose rapamycin improved brain blood flow in healthy middle-aged adults carrying the high-risk APOE4 gene variant, with women showing the strongest benefits. Because declining blood flow can occur years before Alzheimer's symptoms appear, the discovery raises hopes for preventing or delaying the disease before memory loss begins.
top.text: A drug commonly used to prevent organ transplant rejection may offer an unexpected new approach to protecting people at increased risk of Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at the University of Missouri have discovered that rapamycin, a medication also studied for its effects on aging, can improve blood flow in the brains of middle-aged adults who carry a gene variant linked to Alzheimer's. The findings could help scientists develop strategies to address Alzheimer's risk long before memory problems appear. The research also adds to the University of Missouri's growing contributions to understanding and potentially preventing the most common form of dementia. The study was led by Ai-Ling Lin, a professor in the university's School of Medicine and an investigator at the Roy Blunt NextGen Precision Health building. Her work focuses on identifying changes in the brain that occur before Alzheimer's symptoms develop and finding ways to intervene early. A major focus of Lin's research is the APOE4 gene variant, which is associated with a substantially increased risk of developing Alzheimer's disease later in life. People who carry APOE4 can experience reduced blood flow in certain areas of the brain years before they begin having noticeable memory difficulties. Because these circulation changes can occur so early, researchers believe they could provide an important warning sign of increased Alzheimer's risk. Lin's latest findings suggest that improving brain circulation with an existing medication may be one way to address these early changes. "Alzheimer's tends to happen more in older people, especially for those with APOE4," Lin said. "If we can slow down aging in the brain for those people most at risk, maybe we can reduce the risk of them developing Alzheimer's disease." Rapamycin is already used in medicine to prevent the immune system from rejecting transplanted organs and to treat certain rare conditions. However, researchers have also been investigating its potential to slow biological aging and protect the brain. Before joining the University of Missouri, Lin conducted experiments involving mice that carried APOE4. Her earlier research showed that rapamycin could slow brain aging and increase blood flow in these animals. Those results prompted an important question: Could rapamycin produce similar benefits in people who have a genetic predisposition to Alzheimer's but have not yet developed the disease? To investigate, Lin studied healthy adults between the ages of 45 and 65, including people who carried APOE4 and others who did not. All participants received a low daily dose of rapamycin for four weeks. When researchers examined the results, they found a notable difference between the two groups. Brain blood flow improved among participants carrying APOE4, but the same benefit was not observed in those without the gene variant. This suggests that rapamycin may have particular potential for people whose genetics place them at greater risk of Alzheimer's. Although the study did not establish whether the treatment could prevent Alzheimer's or preserve memory over time, the improved circulation offers a promising direction for future research. Women With the Alzheimer's Risk Gene Saw the Greatest Benefits Another intriguing finding emerged when the researchers examined differences between male and female participants. Women carrying APOE4 experienced the largest improvements in brain blood flow following treatment. That result may be especially important because women account for nearly two-thirds of people living with Alzheimer's disease. "We also found that females with APOE4 saw the greatest improvement in brain blood flow, which is significant given that nearly two-thirds of people with Alzheimer's are women," she said. "This research is an example of precision medicine, as we work to identify who can benefit from this drug the most." The results highlight the potential of precision medicine, an approach that considers individual characteristics, including genetics, when determining which treatments may be most effective. Rather than assuming that a medication will benefit everyone equally, researchers hope to identify the people most likely to respond. Lin, who is also a professor in the university's College of Arts and Science, credits Mizzou's collaborative research environment with helping advance discoveries like these. At the Roy Blunt NextGen Precision Health building, scientists and medical professionals work together in the same facility. This collaboration is designed to help move promising laboratory findings into human clinical studies more quickly. The latest results provide an encouraging starting point for investigating whether rapamycin could eventually help delay or reduce Alzheimer's risk in genetically vulnerable individuals. More research will be needed to determine whether the changes in brain blood flow lead to lasting improvements in brain health or a lower likelihood of developing the disease. The study, "EXPRESS: Rapamycin increases cerebral blood flow and modulates metabolic, inflammatory, and microbiome profiles in healthy middle-aged APOE4 carriers: a pilot single-arm trial" was published in Journal of Cerebral Blood Flow & Metabolism . top.title: Magic mushrooms rewire the brain in a way scientists didn't expect
top.summary: A surprising discovery reveals how psilocybin, the active compound in magic mushrooms, rapidly reshapes the brain by creating new neural connections and strengthening them. Researchers found that the drug behaves differently in healthy and chronically stressed mice, potentially helping repair brain circuits damaged by prolonged stress. Most intriguingly, they identified a way to trigger this brain rewiring without the behavioral response associated with psychedelic effects.
top.text: A new study from the University of California, Santa Cruz, has revealed how psilocybin, the psychedelic substance found in "magic mushrooms," changes the brain by reorganizing connections between nerve cells. The findings could eventually help scientists develop treatments for mental health conditions that capture some of psilocybin's potential benefits without producing hallucinations. The research, published October 15 in Nature Neuroscience , found that psilocybin rapidly encourages brain cells to form new connections and helps those connections mature. At the same time, it promotes the removal of certain older connections, suggesting that its effects involve more than simply increasing communication between neurons. Experiments in mice also revealed something especially intriguing. The researchers were able to separate the cellular changes responsible for this rewiring from a behavioral response commonly associated with psychedelic effects. This suggests that some of psilocybin's effects on brain structure may be achievable without the hallucinations typically associated with the drug. The discovery could provide a foundation for developing medications that enhance the brain's ability to adapt and reorganize itself, a property known as neuroplasticity. Such treatments might eventually offer new approaches for depression, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and other psychiatric conditions. The team also identified a particular group of neurons in the cerebral cortex that plays an essential role in psilocybin's effects on brain connections. Importantly, the researchers discovered that the drug does not affect every brain in the same way. Its influence depends partly on whether the brain has previously experienced chronic stress. "I consider this work a major advance, particularly in our understanding of how psilocybin reshapes neural circuits and its potential implications for treating mental disorders," said senior author Yi Zuo, professor of molecular, cell, and developmental biology at UC Santa Cruz. Scientific interest in psychedelic drugs has changed dramatically over the past century. During the middle of the 20th century, substances such as psilocybin and LSD attracted attention from Western researchers because of their powerful effects on perception, consciousness, and mood. Early studies suggested these compounds might have applications in psychiatric treatment. However, scientific investigations slowed substantially after the United States passed the Controlled Substances Act in 1970, which imposed strict restrictions on these substances. In recent years, researchers have renewed their interest in psychedelics, particularly their ability to produce rapid and potentially lasting changes in brain function. Scientists sometimes describe these compounds as "psychoplastogens" because they can stimulate neuroplasticity after a single dose. Neuroplasticity refers to the brain's capacity to change its structure and activity by forming, strengthening, reorganizing, or removing connections between neurons. This property is particularly interesting for mental health treatment because conditions such as depression can involve disruptions in the circuits responsible for regulating mood, emotions, and behavior. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has previously recognized the therapeutic potential of psychedelic research by granting Breakthrough Therapy designations to substances including psilocybin and MDMA. These designations are intended to accelerate the development and review of promising treatments for serious medical conditions. In September 2026, the FDA took another step toward evaluating psychedelic treatments by organizing a public hearing titled "Considerations for Potential Future Therapeutic Use of Psychedelic Drugs." Experts discussed how healthcare professionals administering psychedelic treatments should be qualified, how potential risks could be managed through Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) programs, and how future clinical trials should be designed. As regulators examine ways psychedelic treatments might eventually become part of mainstream healthcare, researchers are increasingly focused on understanding exactly what these substances do to the brain. Identifying the cellular mechanisms behind their effects could help scientists develop treatments that are both effective and safer to administer. To investigate how psilocybin changes brain structure, the UC Santa Cruz team used an advanced imaging method called two-photon microscopy. This technology allows scientists to observe extremely small structures inside living tissue with remarkable detail. Using it, the researchers followed individual connections on neurons in living mice over several weeks, allowing them to see how those structures changed after psilocybin treatment. Their attention centered on tiny projections called dendritic spines. These structures extend from neurons and receive messages from neighboring nerve cells. They help form synapses, the specialized junctions through which neurons communicate. Synapses are essential for processing information and supporting functions such as learning, memory, and emotional regulation. Changes in their number, strength, and organization can alter the way information travels through the brain. Within just 24 hours of psilocybin administration, the researchers observed a substantial increase in newly forming dendritic spines. But the drug did more than encourage new connections to appear. It also helped them develop into more mature structures at an unusually rapid pace. Normally, newly formed spines often begin as small, immature structures described as "stubby." Many remain unstable and disappear before becoming fully developed connections. After psilocybin treatment, however, a much larger proportion developed into structures with a distinctive "mushroom" appearance. These mature spines are generally more stable and contain higher concentrations of receptors that receive chemical signals from neighboring neurons. Because of these features, mature spines can support stronger and more persistent communication between brain cells, potentially contributing to lasting changes in circuits involved in memory and mood. For lead author Jacob Baker, one of the biggest questions is whether these structural changes require the intense psychedelic experience typically produced by psilocybin. "Psychedelics are fascinating compounds because they have the potential to profoundly transform who we are by reshaping the neural circuits in our brains," said Baker, a Ph.D. student in Zuo's lab. "These newly formed connections can integrate into existing neural circuitry and persist over time, leaving a lasting structural trace of psilocybin's effects on the brain." One of the study's most revealing findings was that psilocybin's influence on brain connections changed depending on whether the mice had experienced prolonged stress. In healthy mice, psilocybin initially stimulated the formation of new dendritic spines. Over the following three weeks, however, the number of connections gradually moved back toward its previous level. This happened partly because the brain eliminated some connections that had existed before treatment. Rather than simply accumulating additional synapses, the healthy brain appeared to reorganize its existing circuitry while maintaining an overall balance. The researchers observed a different response in mice exposed to chronic stress. To investigate this, they used an unpredictable mild stress model, which exposes animals to varying low-intensity stressors and produces changes that resemble certain features of human depression. top.title: Scientists discover that some “unhealthy” diets can boost cancer immunotherapy in mice
top.summary: In a surprising discovery, scientists found that certain diets associated with obesity can make cancer immunotherapy more effective in mice, challenging traditional assumptions about diet and cancer treatment. The findings suggest that the secret may lie in how food interacts with gut bacteria to strengthen the immune system's response to cancer.
top.text: Scientists have uncovered an unexpected connection between diet and cancer treatment. In a surprising finding, certain diets typically considered "unhealthy" or "fattening" actually improved responses to a common form of cancer immunotherapy in mice. The discovery suggests that the success of cancer treatment may depend not only on which bacteria live in the gut, but also on the foods that help those bacteria thrive. "There is a synergistic relationship between the bacteria that reside in our GI tract, and the food we eat," said Daniela Quail, Associate Professor in the Department of Physiology and Principal Investigator at the Rosalind & Morris Goodman Cancer Institute. "Even with the right composition of bacteria in your gut, the foods you eat to nourish those populations can determine whether or not you respond to treatment," said Quail. Quail co-led the research, which examined how diet influences the effectiveness of immune checkpoint inhibitors. These widely used immunotherapy drugs help the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. Other senior researchers involved in the study included McGill scientist Logan Walsh and CR-CHUM collaborators Bertrand Routy and Arielle Elkrief. The findings were published in Nature . One of the most unexpected discoveries was that some diets associated with weight gain appeared to make immunotherapy more effective, challenging assumptions about the relationship between nutrition and cancer treatment. "Our findings were surprising because they highlighted a benefit of some obesogenic diets," she said. "That tells us the relationship between diet and cancer treatment is more complex than a simple message to eat healthy and exercise." However, the researchers emphasize that these results should not encourage cancer patients to consume diets that promote obesity. Excess weight carries established health risks, and the findings do not demonstrate that adopting such diets would improve cancer treatment in humans. Instead, the scientists want to understand how different foods influence the gut microbiome, the enormous community of trillions of bacteria that inhabit the digestive system. Identifying the mechanisms responsible for the improved treatment responses could eventually help researchers develop safer ways to make cancer immunotherapy more effective. The investigation grew out of a longstanding puzzle in cancer research known as the "obesity paradox." Obesity is generally linked to a greater risk of developing cancer and dying from the disease. Yet several studies have found that cancer patients with a higher body mass index (BMI) sometimes respond more favorably to immune checkpoint inhibitors. To investigate this apparent contradiction, the research team tested 12 different diets in mice. Surprisingly, some diets associated with obesity improved the animals' responses to immunotherapy, even when they were consumed for relatively short periods. These results suggest that the apparent treatment advantage associated with obesity may not be primarily caused by excess body weight. Instead, the explanation could involve the combined influence of diet and gut bacteria on the immune system. By uncovering how these interactions affect cancer treatment, researchers hope to identify new approaches that reproduce the beneficial effects without exposing patients to the health risks associated with obesity. The study, "Diet-microbiome synergy underlies obesity-associated immunotherapy efficacy," was published in Nature by McGill PhD graduate Lysanne Desharnais, Daniela Quail, and their collaborators. top.title: Kids who eat more ultra-processed foods show a troubling brain response
top.summary: A new study suggests that ultra-processed foods may influence children's developing brains in ways that encourage weight gain. Researchers from USC studied 46 children ages 7 to 10 and found that those who ate more ultra-processed foods showed stronger activity in the brain's reward system when viewing tempting foods like cookies and French fries. These heightened brain responses were linked to greater increases in body fat and body mass index (BMI) one year later, suggesting that the brain's sensitivity to food cues may help explain why ultra-processed diets are associated with obesity.
top.text: Children who consume more ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may have stronger brain responses to tempting foods, potentially helping explain why these products are associated with weight gain. A new study published in JAMA Network Open found that children who ate more of these foods showed heightened activity in the brain's reward system when looking at pictures of appetizing foods. Those stronger responses were also associated with increases in body fat over the following year. Ultra-processed foods include many everyday products, such as breakfast cereals, packaged bread, and instant soups. They are manufactured to be appealing, convenient, and able to remain fresh for extended periods. Many contain artificial sweeteners, coloring agents, and other ingredients rarely used in home cooking. These products make up a substantial portion of children's diets, accounting for approximately 67% of the calories consumed by children in the United States. Previous research has associated ultra-processed food consumption with obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. However, scientists are still trying to understand the biological processes that might explain these connections. The new investigation, supported in part by the National Institutes of Health, combined magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), dietary assessments, and measurements of children's body composition to explore whether the brain's response to food could play a role. "Children's brains are still developing, habits are still forming and food preferences are still being made. It's an important period where the brain is very sensitive to food and the food environment," said the study's senior author, Kathleen A. Page, MD, professor of medicine and pediatrics and co-chief of the Division of Endocrinology and Diabetes at the Keck School of Medicine of USC. "We're particularly interested in understanding these processes in children, because we believe that intervening early could make a real difference." To investigate these connections, the research team studied 46 children between the ages of seven and 10 who were enrolled in the ongoing BrainChild study, which examines factors contributing to diabetes and obesity. Every participant had a healthy weight when the research began, giving scientists an opportunity to investigate potential warning signs before excess weight developed. At the start of the study, the children underwent brain scans while looking at pictures of appealing foods (such as cookies or French fries). Researchers also gathered information about their diets and recorded several health measurements, including body mass index (BMI), body fat percentage, and waist circumference. After one year, the team measured these physical characteristics again to identify changes. The brain scans revealed a notable pattern. Children who consumed larger amounts of ultra-processed foods showed greater activity in the dorsal striatum when viewing food pictures. This part of the brain helps regulate reward and motivation, making it particularly relevant to how people respond to desirable foods. Importantly, children with stronger responses in this brain region also tended to experience greater increases in BMI and body fat percentage over the next year. The findings suggest that heightened sensitivity to food cues may be one factor connecting ultra-processed diets with subsequent weight gain. By the end of the study, children who consumed more ultra-processed foods generally had higher BMI, greater body fat percentage, and larger waist circumference. The researchers then examined whether differences in brain activity could help account for these associations. When they adjusted their analysis to consider the children's responses in the dorsal striatum, the relationship between ultra-processed food intake and BMI became 31% weaker. The corresponding association with body fat percentage decreased by 44%. These reductions suggest that the brain's reward response may help explain part of the relationship between ultra-processed food consumption and changes in body composition. Although the results do not demonstrate that these foods directly alter brain function, they provide a possible biological explanation for an association that has been observed in previous research. "This study goes beyond just understanding that UPFs affect weight gain," Page said. "It actually gives us insight into the neurobiological underpinnings by which these foods may be linked to body composition over time." The researchers caution that improving children's diets cannot depend entirely on individual families. Ultra-processed products are often inexpensive, widely available, and easy to prepare, making them practical choices for households facing financial or time constraints. "Changing the food environment to help people access healthier, more minimally processed foods is an important part of the solution," Page said. There are also important limitations to consider. Because the study was observational, it cannot determine whether eating ultra-processed foods directly causes heightened brain activity or increases in body weight. The findings establish relationships between these factors, but additional research is needed to determine whether one causes another. Page hopes to address that question in a future intervention study. The proposed research would provide children who regularly consume ultra-processed foods with more minimally processed alternatives. Scientists could then examine whether changing their diets affects how their brains respond to food images and whether any differences are associated with reduced weight gain. Meanwhile, the BrainChild study will continue tracking participants as they move through puberty and into early adulthood. By monitoring brain development, body composition, dietary patterns, and general health over time, researchers hope to gain a clearer picture of how childhood nutrition may influence long-term health. top.title: Scientists discover a surprising brain benefit of eating peanuts every day
top.summary: A surprising new study suggests that eating peanuts every day could help support brain health and memory in older adults. Researchers found that consuming about two servings of unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts daily for 16 weeks improved insulin responsiveness in brain regions important for memory, a function that often weakens with age and has been linked to Alzheimer's disease.
top.text: Eating peanuts every day may offer surprising benefits for the aging brain. Researchers at Maastricht University Medical Center in the Netherlands have found that regularly consuming unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts can improve how certain brain regions respond to insulin in older adults. The findings come from the Institute of Nutrition and Translational Research in Metabolism (NUTRIM) and were published in the peer-reviewed journal Food & Function . Although insulin is best known for regulating blood sugar, it also plays an essential role in the brain. It helps nerve cells grow, survive, and communicate with one another, supporting memory and other cognitive abilities. Healthy insulin signaling may also help protect against processes associated with Alzheimer's disease. After participants consumed peanuts daily for 16 weeks, researchers observed improved insulin responsiveness in a group of brain regions in the right hemisphere. These included portions of the lingual gyrus, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and posterior cingulate gyrus, all of which contribute to memory-related processes. "The hormone insulin plays an important role in the brain, where it supports memory and other cognitive processes. As people age, the brain may become less responsive to insulin, which has been linked to age-related cognitive decline," says Dr. Peter Joris, the study's senior author and an associate professor in the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences, NUTRIM, Maastricht University Medical Center. "Our study found that daily peanut consumption beneficially affected insulin responsiveness in memory-related brain regions in older adults. These findings suggest that enhanced regional brain insulin responsiveness may contribute to the cognitive benefits of unsalted, skin-roasted peanut intake." The study included 31 healthy adults between the ages of 60 and 75. During the peanut consumption phase, participants ate 60 grams (approximately two servings) of peanuts each day for 16 weeks. Researchers used a randomized, controlled crossover trial, a rigorous study design that allowed them to compare the effects of eating peanuts with those of avoiding them. The new findings build on earlier research by Joris published in 2025. That investigation found that consuming peanuts for 16 weeks increased overall cerebral blood flow (CBF) by 3.6% and improved verbal memory performance by 5.8%. Cerebral blood flow measures how much blood circulates through the brain, carrying oxygen and nutrients that brain cells need to function properly. It is an important indicator of the health of the brain's blood vessels. Those earlier results appeared in the peer-reviewed journal Clinical Nutrition . One distinguishing feature of the NUTRIM research was its combination of a carefully controlled dietary intervention lasting several months with sophisticated brain imaging technology. To examine changes in brain function, researchers used arterial spin labeling magnetic resonance imaging (ASL-MRI), a technique that measures blood flow in different regions of the brain. They evaluated insulin responsiveness by tracking changes in regional cerebral blood flow after insulin was administered through the nose. The team also used abdominal MRI scans to measure fat accumulation in the liver, known as intrahepatic lipid (IHL) content. Cognitive abilities were assessed using the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB), a standardized collection of computerized tests. Researchers believe several components of peanuts may contribute to their observed effects on brain health, rather than any single nutrient being responsible. "Multiple nutrients present in peanuts, including unsaturated fats, dietary fiber, vitamins and minerals and bioactive phytochemicals, could potentially contribute to the observed brain benefits," says Joris. "Peanuts are also a good source of plant-based protein and are especially rich in L-arginine. L-arginine is a key precursor of nitric oxide (NO), which has been reported to facilitate learning and memory performance." To ensure participants consumed a consistent amount, researchers supplied premeasured packets of skin-roasted peanuts throughout the peanut intervention period. Participants were instructed to eat their peanuts in the morning or afternoon, but they could choose how to incorporate them into their daily routine. They could consume the entire portion at once, divide it into smaller amounts throughout the day, or include the peanuts in their meals. During the control phase, participants avoided peanuts entirely. After 16 weeks, they switched to the opposite study condition, allowing researchers to compare brain health measurements under both dietary approaches. The study was led by principal investigator Associate Professor Dr. Peter J. Joris and conducted by Ph.D. candidate Lucia Kerkhof of the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences at Maastricht University Medical Center. According to the researchers, the foundation had no involvement in designing or conducting the study, analyzing or interpreting the results, or preparing the manuscript. top.title: AI helps Stanford scientists discover a “natural Ozempic” with a surprising advantage
top.summary: Stanford researchers have discovered an AI-identified natural molecule that dramatically suppresses appetite and promotes fat loss in animals, potentially offering an Ozempic-like weight-loss treatment without common digestive side effects or significant muscle loss. Called BRP, the molecule reduced food intake by up to 50% and targets a different brain pathway, raising hopes for a more precise obesity treatment if future human trials prove successful.
top.text: Scientists at Stanford Medicine have identified a naturally occurring molecule that could lead to a new generation of weight loss medications. Early animal experiments suggest that it can suppress appetite and promote fat loss much like semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic, while potentially avoiding some of the drug's troublesome side effects. The molecule, known as BRP, works differently from existing treatments. Rather than affecting several organs throughout the body, it appears to act more selectively on a part of the brain responsible for controlling hunger and metabolism. This more focused approach could eventually help people lose weight without experiencing problems such as nausea, constipation, or substantial muscle loss. Researchers discovered BRP with the help of artificial intelligence, which allowed them to search through thousands of possible biological compounds. The findings were promising enough that the scientists began preparing for the next major step: determining whether the molecule is safe and effective in humans. "The receptors targeted by semaglutide are found in the brain but also in the gut, pancreas and other tissues," said assistant professor of pathology Katrin Svensson, PhD. "That's why Ozempic has widespread effects including slowing the movement of food through the digestive tract and lowering blood sugar levels. In contrast, BRP appears to act specifically in the hypothalamus, which controls appetite and metabolism." The hypothalamus is a small but essential region deep within the brain. Among its many responsibilities, it helps regulate hunger, energy use, body temperature, and other functions needed to maintain the body's internal balance. Because it plays such a central role in appetite, it is an important target for researchers developing obesity treatments. Semaglutide works by imitating a hormone called glucagon-like peptide 1, or GLP-1. This hormone helps regulate blood sugar and signals that influence hunger and feelings of fullness. However, GLP-1 receptors are distributed throughout several parts of the body, which helps explain why medications that activate them can produce effects beyond appetite suppression. BRP appears to take another route. Although it influences some of the same broad metabolic functions as semaglutide, it activates different populations of brain cells. Scientists believe this distinction could make it possible to control hunger more precisely while reducing unwanted effects elsewhere in the body. Svensson, who served as senior author of the study, published in Nature , has also cofounded a company to advance BRP toward human clinical trials. The research was led by senior research scientist Laetitia Coassolo, PhD. Finding BRP required solving a problem that has long complicated the search for new hormones. The human body produces enormous numbers of small protein fragments, but only a fraction have important biological functions. Identifying the ones that influence appetite or metabolism can be extremely difficult. Many hormones begin as larger, inactive proteins known as prohormones. Specialized enzymes cut these proteins into smaller pieces called peptides. Some of those peptides become chemical messengers that help coordinate processes such as energy metabolism, appetite, and organ function. A single prohormone can be cut in several different places, potentially producing numerous peptides with distinct effects. The challenge is determining which fragments are biologically useful and which are simply leftovers from normal protein processing. The important peptide hormones (which are relatively rare) can be difficult to distinguish from the much larger collection of ordinary protein fragments. Traditional approaches often involve extracting proteins from biological tissues and analyzing them with techniques such as mass spectrometry. This method identifies molecules by measuring characteristics related to their mass, but the sheer number of possible peptides makes searching for new hormones a demanding process. The Stanford team decided to approach the problem differently. They concentrated on an enzyme called prohormone convertase 1/3, which cuts prohormones at particular amino acid sequences and has previously been linked to human obesity. Amino acids are the molecular building blocks of proteins, and their arrangement helps determine where enzymes can cut them. One of the hormones produced through this process is GLP-1, the same hormone whose effects semaglutide mimics. The researchers reasoned that other peptides generated through similar processing might also help regulate appetite and energy use. To accelerate the search, the scientists created a computer algorithm called Peptide Predictor. Instead of physically isolating and examining hundreds of thousands of peptides, the program analyzed the roughly 20,000 genes that encode human proteins, looking for sequences where the enzyme was likely to make cuts. The team then refined the results by concentrating on genes associated with proteins released outside cells, a common characteristic of hormones. They also required each candidate protein to contain at least four potential cutting sites. These filters reduced an enormous collection of possibilities to 373 prohormones, making experimental testing much more practical. "The algorithm was absolutely key to our findings," Svensson said. Peptide Predictor estimated that the enzyme could produce 2,683 distinct peptides from those 373 proteins. From this collection, Svensson and Coassolo selected candidates that appeared particularly likely to influence brain activity. The researchers eventually tested 100 peptides, including GLP-1, using nerve cells grown in the laboratory. Their goal was to find substances capable of stimulating neuronal activity, an early indication that a peptide might influence important brain processes. GLP-1 performed strongly in the laboratory tests, increasing neuronal activity to three times the level observed in untreated control cells. One previously unrecognized peptide, however, produced an even more striking response. Consisting of just 12 amino acids, it increased neuronal activity tenfold compared with the controls. The researchers named the molecule BRP after the larger protein from which it originates, BPM/retinoic acid inducible neural specific 2, or BRINP2 (BRINP2-related-peptide). That unusually powerful response made BRP a promising candidate for further investigation. The next question was whether stimulating laboratory-grown brain cells would translate into meaningful changes in appetite and body weight in living animals. The team tested BRP in lean mice and minipigs (which more closely mirror human metabolism and eating patterns than mice do). Before the animals were fed, researchers administered BRP through an injection into the muscle. The results were striking. During the following hour, the treated animals consumed up to 50% less food than expected, suggesting that BRP could strongly influence hunger. The scientists then examined whether repeated treatment could produce sustained changes in body weight. Obese mice received daily BRP injections for 14 days. By the end of the experiment, the treated mice had lost an average of 3 grams, while untreated control mice had gained approximately 3 grams. Importantly, nearly all the weight lost by the BRP-treated mice came from body fat rather than muscle. Preserving muscle is an important goal in obesity treatment because muscle tissue supports strength, mobility, and metabolic health. The treated animals also showed improvements in glucose and insulin tolerance. These measurements reflect how effectively the body handles sugar and responds to insulin, the hormone that helps move glucose from the bloodstream into cells. top.summary: If you can remember your first sip of coffee, the memory might not be a pleasant one. Coffee's bitter flavor is one we naturally steer clear of. So how do coffee fans learn to love it? top.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
top.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.
top.text: Crown-of-thorns starfish (COTS) are among the most feared creatures on coral reefs. Covered in sharp, toxin-filled spines, these predators are notorious for consuming coral and leaving widespread destruction in their wake. However, new research from the University of Sydney suggests these infamous reef destroyers may also have a surprisingly beneficial side. When their populations remain under control, crown-of-thorns starfish can help maintain healthy coral communities and support greater biodiversity. Native to Australia's Great Barrier Reef, these coral-eating starfish have caused enormous damage during population explosions. Since the 1960s, the reef has experienced four major outbreaks, occurring roughly every 15 years. Declining numbers of natural predators, including tritons and several species of reef fish, have made the Great Barrier Reef and other marine ecosystems more vulnerable to these destructive events. Scientists Discover That Coral Often Survives Starfish Attacks In a study published in Ecology and Evolution, researchers investigated what happens to coral after crown-of-thorns starfish feed on it. The team examined feeding scars and remaining living tissue at the University of Sydney's One Tree Island Research Station, located on the Great Barrier Reef. The study sites were within protected areas where healthy fish populations help keep starfish numbers under control. Unlike other parts of the reef that experience devastating outbreaks, these locations maintain relatively low populations of crown-of-thorns starfish. The results revealed an unexpected pattern. A team led by Dr. Shawna Foo found that living coral tissue survived nearly 75 percent of the observed feeding events. "At One Tree Reef, COTS appear to consume a relatively consistent amount of coral during each meal and move on, rather than demolishing the entire coral colony," said Dr. Foo, a University of Sydney Horizon Fellow in the School of Life and Environmental Sciences. "This meant live coral tissue remnants were frequently left behind." The discovery suggests that small populations of crown-of-thorns starfish may play an important role in maintaining the balance of coral reef ecosystems. Some coral species grow quickly and can take over large areas, limiting the space available to slower-growing varieties. By feeding on these dominant species, crown-of-thorns starfish may create opportunities for other corals to survive and establish themselves. The researchers found that surviving fragments of fast-growing Acroporidae corals did not regenerate over the areas damaged by starfish feeding. In contrast, regrowth occurred primarily among slower-growing Montipora and Porites corals. "By feeding on fast-growing corals such as Acropora, low-density COTS populations create space for slower-growing coral species to persist, helping to increase coral diversity," Dr. Foo said. This finding challenges the idea that all coral consumption by crown-of-thorns starfish is harmful. Under the right conditions, their feeding behavior may actually prevent a few dominant coral species from taking over the reef. Despite these potential benefits, researchers caution that large outbreaks of crown-of-thorns starfish remain a serious threat. When their numbers increase dramatically, they can destroy extensive areas of coral, leaving reefs struggling to recover. The key difference is whether starfish populations remain at naturally manageable levels or grow into destructive outbreaks. "It's important to distinguish between COTS populations performing their natural role as coral predators and outbreaks causing sustained reef decline." Although the research was conducted mainly in protected areas with healthy fish populations and little risk of major outbreaks, the findings could help scientists and conservation managers improve strategies for controlling crown-of-thorns starfish. In particular, the results suggest that removing every starfish may not be the best approach once an outbreak has been brought under control. "The implications of our work can help us decide when and why culling should occur and the ecological endpoint of a cull. Once an outbreak is suppressed, the goal should not necessarily be to eliminate COTS entirely. Culling needs to be complemented by strong marine management to protect COTS predators and keep COTS populations in check." Research co-author Professor Maria Byrne connected the findings to a well-established ecological concept. "The results are consistent with the intermediate disturbance hypothesis, an important framework in ecology and conservation." According to this hypothesis, ecosystems can benefit from occasional, moderate disturbances that prevent any single species from becoming too dominant. The research suggests that crown-of-thorns starfish may be an example of this natural balancing process. While uncontrolled outbreaks can devastate coral reefs, smaller populations may help maintain the diversity that makes these ecosystems so valuable. Materials provided by University of Sydney . top.title: Extra weight may be aging your brain faster than you think
top.summary: A major 24-year study involving more than 8,200 adults suggests that excess body weight may accelerate brain aging, leading to faster declines in memory, concentration, and decision-making skills. The connection was particularly strong among people over 65, raising concerns about the long-term effects of obesity on brain health.
top.text: Carrying excess weight may affect more than physical health. New research from the University of Georgia suggests that having a higher body mass index may also speed up cognitive decline, potentially causing memory and thinking abilities to deteriorate more quickly with age. Some cognitive changes are a natural part of getting older. Remembering information, thinking clearly, and processing new details can become more difficult over time. For healthy adults, however, these changes are usually relatively mild and develop gradually. The new findings suggest that excess body weight may accelerate this process. Researchers found that people with higher body mass index (BMI) experienced faster declines in memory, overall cognitive performance, and executive functioning. These abilities are essential for everyday activities such as concentrating, planning, organizing tasks, and regulating emotions. To investigate the connection, the research team analyzed data from a nationally representative study that tracked more than 8,200 adults over age 50 for 24 years. The results revealed a consistent relationship between body weight and cognitive health. Each one-point increase in BMI was associated with a faster rate of cognitive decline, suggesting that even relatively small differences in body weight could matter over time. The association was strongest at the eighth year of the study, and adults older than 65 showed the most pronounced effects. Despite the concerning findings, researchers also identified a potentially encouraging opportunity to protect brain health. Managing body weight may help slow cognitive decline, with possible benefits becoming apparent within just two years. "We found that if people managed their weight, they could significantly lower their rate of cognitive decline in just two years," said Suhang Song, the study's lead author and an assistant professor at the University of Georgia's College of Public Health. "That makes BMI one of the most easily modifiable risk factors when it comes to aging well." Obesity, generally defined as a BMI of 30 or higher, has been associated with poorer brain health. However, scientists are still working to understand exactly why carrying excess body weight may interfere with memory and other cognitive abilities. Several biological processes could help explain the connection. Excess weight may promote inflammation, impair blood circulation, and contribute to insulin resistance. Together, these changes could increase the likelihood of cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease, and other forms of dementia. The findings are particularly relevant given how widespread obesity has become in the United States. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, approximately two in five Americans meet the criteria for obesity when BMI is used as the sole measure. Some scientists argue that BMI alone does not provide a complete picture of obesity. They support a broader definition that also considers waist measurements and medical conditions associated with excess weight. Using those additional criteria, the estimated proportion of Americans classified as having obesity rises to 75%. The potential connection between obesity and cognitive decline is especially concerning as dementia becomes increasingly common. More than 7 million Americans currently live with dementia, and researchers expect that number to double by 2050. Although the study does not establish that excess weight directly causes cognitive decline, its findings highlight body weight as a potentially important factor in maintaining cognitive health. Because weight can be managed, researchers believe it could offer an opportunity to reduce the risk of worsening memory and thinking abilities as people grow older. "There are no cures for dementia," Song said, "which is why it is critical to identify and address any modifiable risk factors we can find to prevent it." The research was published in the Journal of Neurology . Coauthors from the University of Georgia College of Public Health include Meng Hsuan Sung, Zhuo Chen, Janani Rajbhandari, Grace Bagwell Adams, Mahmud Khan, Ye Shen, and Xiao Song. Qianhui Xu and Xia Song also contributed to the study. Materials provided by University of Georgia . top.title: Scientists reverse liver cell aging and cut Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half
top.summary: A surprising discovery suggests that rejuvenating the liver could help protect against Alzheimer’s disease and heart disease. USC researchers found that an experimental drug restored aging liver cells in rats, cutting levels of an Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half and bringing bad cholesterol down to youthful levels. The treatment also revived a previously unknown communication system that helps liver cells remove harmful substances from the bloodstream.
top.text: The liver may hold an unexpected key to fighting two of the most serious diseases associated with aging: Alzheimer's disease and heart disease. Scientists have discovered that restoring the function of aging liver cells can dramatically reduce harmful substances in the bloodstream, raising the possibility of treating diseases that affect organs far beyond the liver itself. In a new study involving older rats, researchers at the Keck School of Medicine of USC found that an experimental drug called cinaciguat reversed important signs of aging in specialized liver cells. After just two weeks of treatment, levels of amyloid beta, a protein associated with Alzheimer's disease, dropped by half. Levels of LDL, commonly called bad cholesterol, also returned to those seen in younger animals. The findings, published in the Journal of Biological Chemistry , also revealed a previously unknown way that liver cells communicate with one another. This discovery could help scientists develop treatments that restore the liver's ability to remove potentially harmful substances from the blood, possibly reducing the risk of Alzheimer's disease and atherosclerosis, a condition in which fatty deposits accumulate inside arteries. Although Alzheimer's primarily affects the brain, scientists are increasingly interested in how other organs might influence the disease. The liver plays a central role in filtering the blood and removing unwanted compounds, including substances that may contribute to disease when they accumulate. The USC findings suggest that restoring this natural cleaning process could offer a different approach to preventing certain age-related illnesses. However, the results have so far been demonstrated only in rats, and additional studies are needed to establish whether the same benefits occur in humans. "We need to do further translational work to see whether our findings might point to new therapies," said corresponding author Laurie DeLeve, MD, PhD, professor and vice chair for scientific affairs in the USC Department of Medicine. "We're hopeful, though, because the findings line up with a lot of epidemiological results showing age as a major risk factor for Alzheimer's and atherosclerosis, and liver damage as a risk factor for Alzheimer's." Targeting the liver could be particularly valuable in Alzheimer's research, where efforts to develop treatments acting directly in the brain have faced an estimated 98% failure rate in clinical trials. One major obstacle is the blood-brain barrier, a protective system that limits which substances can enter the brain from the bloodstream. While this barrier helps shield the brain from harmful compounds, it also makes delivering certain medications extremely difficult. "If we're right that the liver is impactful, what do we do about that?" said first author Sam de Leve, MA, a USC lab technician and child of Laurie DeLeve. "Rather than trying to get a drug through the blood-brain barrier, which is obnoxiously difficult, we could direct drugs to the liver, an organ where there might be more therapeutic impact and certainly an easier job of drug delivery." To understand how liver aging affects the bloodstream, the researchers focused on a relatively understudied group of cells known as liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs). These cells form the lining of tiny blood vessels inside the liver. Unlike most blood vessel walls, they contain numerous microscopic openings that function somewhat like the holes in a sieve. These openings allow larger molecules circulating in the blood to reach neighboring cells called hepatocytes, which carry out much of the liver's work processing and removing substances from the body. As the liver ages, the openings in LSECs gradually become smaller or disappear. This makes it harder for certain large molecules to reach the cells responsible for clearing them, allowing more of these substances to remain in circulation. One substance affected by this change is amyloid beta. This protein is especially important in Alzheimer's research because it can accumulate in the brain and form plaques, one of the disease's defining features. Previous observations showed that the liver becomes less effective at removing amyloid beta as it ages. The researchers suspected that the gradual closing of the openings in LSECs might help explain why more of the protein remains in the bloodstream of older animals. To investigate, they administered cinaciguat to aged rats for two weeks. They then compared the treated animals with two untreated groups, one consisting of older rats and the other of younger rats. The results were striking. Cinaciguat restored the structure and function of the aging LSECs, reopening their microscopic pores and improving their ability to help clear substances from the blood. Amyloid beta concentrations fell by approximately 50%, reaching levels comparable to those in young rats. The untreated older animals showed no similar improvement. The researchers also measured low-density lipoproteins (LDL), often referred to as "bad" cholesterol because elevated levels contribute to fatty deposits inside arteries. Over time, these deposits can restrict blood flow and increase the risk of heart disease. Initially, LDL was included as a comparison measure rather than a substance expected to respond to treatment. Unlike larger molecules, LDL particles are small enough to leave the bloodstream without passing through the microscopic openings in LSECs. The scientists therefore expected cinaciguat to have little or no effect on LDL levels. Instead, they discovered that LDL concentrations in treated older rats also fell to levels observed in young animals. "We said, 'Wait, why did that go down? Clearly, there's more to this story,'" Sam de Leve said. The unexpected finding suggested that the drug was doing more than simply reopening the liver's aging filters. It appeared to be restoring another important aspect of liver function. Because previous research had shown that hepatocytes function better when LSECs are present, the team began examining how these two types of cells communicate. Their investigation uncovered a previously unknown sequence of biochemical signals that helps coordinate the liver's ability to remove substances from the bloodstream. The researchers found that cinaciguat activates an enzyme called soluble guanylate cyclase inside LSECs. This triggers the cells to release a growth factor known as HB-EGF, which sends a signal to nearby hepatocytes. In response, hepatocytes alter their surfaces in ways that allow them to capture more LDL and amyloid beta from the blood. This helps explain why the treatment reduced both substances, even though they do not rely on the same filtering mechanism. Normally, aging interferes with the ability of LSECs to release HB-EGF. Cinaciguat restored this signaling process, allowing the liver cells to communicate more effectively and supporting the removal of substances that otherwise tend to accumulate with age. The discovery identifies a potential new target for future drugs. Rather than focusing exclusively on the physical openings in LSECs, researchers may be able to develop therapies that restore the chemical signals responsible for helping the liver work efficiently. Could Liver Rejuvenation Help Prevent Alzheimer's and Heart Disease? According to the researchers, this is the first study to demonstrate that a drug can fully restore the structure and function of aging LSECs, including their ability to support the clearance of substances from the bloodstream. It is also the first to show that a treatment directed at the liver can bring age-related elevations in circulating amyloid beta and LDL back to youthful levels. These findings raise the possibility that cinaciguat, similar medications, or treatments targeting HB-EGF could eventually be used to counteract certain effects of liver aging. top.title: A Feejee Mermaid on display in Colorado may shock and intrigue – but it’s no longer considered a ‘missing link’ on the evolutionary tree
top.summary: Mermaids have inhabited world folklore and mythology for centuries. Ancient Babylonians worshiped Oannes, a human-fish hybrid; sirens populated Greek mythology; and fairy tales such as "The Little Mermaid" have made this figure a pop culture icon.
top.text: Mermaids have inhabited world folklore and mythology for centuries. Ancient Babylonians worshipped Oannes , a human-fish hybrid; sirens populated Greek mythology ; and fairy tales such as “ The Little Mermaid ” have made this figure a pop culture icon. During the 1800s, American showman P.T. Barnum brought the Feejee Mermaid to the American public. Presented at the American Museum, run by Barnum in Manhattan from 1841 to 1865 , as “ The Greatest Curiosity in the World ” and said to have originated in the “Feejee Islands,” the creature inspired debates about science and evolution. Some people believed it was a missing link in the evolutionary chain between aquatic and terrestrial life. I recently viewed a Feejee Mermaid replica on display at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science as part of the “ Mythic Creatures: Dragons, Unicorns and Mermaids” temporary exhibit . As a folklorist , I’m intrigued by how this mermaid subverted Americans’ expectations that mermaids are alluring and how it sparked an interplay between science and myth. A Feejee Mermaid is a type of traditional art form that originated in Japan and the East Indies more than 400 years ago. It came to Americans in 1842, when Barnum claimed to display a “specimen” at the American Museum in New York City. In the Japanese version, the lower half was a fish attached to an upper half of a monkey or made of papier-mâché. Barnum’s was a mixture of a monkey and a fish, but the replica on display at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science has a papier-mâché upper half. Feejee Mermaids were often preserved by being coated in clay . Mammalian-fish hybrid creatures have a role in Japanese folklore through the ningyo , which are a mermaidlike yokai, a supernatural being thought to have the power to either curse or grant eternal life. Unlike Western mermaids, ningyo were grotesque. The Feejee Mermaid that became part of Barnum’s exhibition was created by a Japanese fisherman in the early 19th century. He claimed to have caught the specimen and said it prophesied a sterility epidemic. The only cure for the townsfolk, the fisherman said, came through owning a picture of the mermaid. Samuel Barrett Eades, an American sailor, purchased the Feejee Mermaid and willed it to his son, who then sold it to Moses Kimball , a curator at the Boston Museum, in 1842. In his autobiography, Barnum details the scheme he devised after Kimball showed him the Feejee Mermaid. Barnum sent letters to newspapers, describing how a “Dr. Griffin,” who was really his hoaxing accomplice Levi Lyman, was in possession of the mermaid skeleton. He further spread the word by distributing thousands of pamphlets throughout New York City that detailed when the mermaid would be on display and highlighted the seductive nature of mermaids. However, when the public arrived at the American Museum, much to their surprise, they found Barnum’s grotesque version. Barnum himself described it as “an ugly dried-up, black-looking diminutive specimen, about three feet long. Its mouth was open, its tail turned over and its arms thrown up, giving it the appearance of having died in great agony.” The Feejee Mermaid on display at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science, and owned by the Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology, may or may not be the one shown by Barnum. The museum says it is a replica. The original was likely destroyed or disfigured in a fire at Barnum’s museum or the Boston Museum. The object on display looks quite different compared to original descriptions of the Feejee Mermaid. As originally shown, it was said to be much more monkeylike, and artistic renderings of it from the period matched Barnum’s descriptions. Feejee Mermaids, as displayed in America, are characteristic of a “ sideshow gaff ” that interested Victorian audiences due to debates about evolution and science. In fact, 18th-century Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus had left space for mermaids in the evolutionary tree . The Feejee Mermaid, as it blended human and animal characteristics, folklore and science, spectacle and empiricism, displays how a monstrous hoax inspired fierce intellectual debates in 19th-century America.

top.title: Drinking 2–3 cups of coffee a day linked to dramatically lower dementia risk
top.summary: Drinking two to three cups of caffeinated coffee daily was linked to a dramatically lower risk of dementia and better cognitive functioning in a study spanning up to 43 years. The benefits appeared regardless of genetic risk, but decaffeinated coffee did not show the same association.
top.text: Your daily cup of coffee may be doing more than helping you wake up in the morning. A long-running study of U.S. adults suggests that drinking caffeinated coffee regularly is associated with a substantially lower risk of dementia and better cognitive health as people age. Researchers found that adults who consumed higher amounts of caffeinated coffee developed dementia at considerably lower rates than those who rarely or never drank it. The findings were based on follow-up periods extending as long as 43 years, offering a valuable look at how everyday drinking habits relate to brain health over time. The strongest associations appeared among people who drank two to three cups of caffeinated coffee each day. Tea consumption was also linked to better cognitive outcomes, although the amount associated with the greatest benefit was somewhat lower. Interestingly, decaffeinated coffee did not show the same benefits, raising questions about whether caffeine itself might help explain the connection. One of the most striking findings involved the difference in dementia rates between regular coffee drinkers and people who consumed little or no coffee. Among U.S. adults who drank higher amounts of caffeinated coffee, researchers recorded 141 dementia cases annually for every 100,000 people. In comparison, the rate was 330 cases per 100,000 people each year among those who rarely or never drank caffeinated coffee. Dementia is a general term for conditions that progressively interfere with memory, thinking, reasoning, and the ability to perform everyday activities. Alzheimer's disease is its most common cause, although several other brain disorders can also lead to dementia. While occasional forgetfulness can be a normal part of aging, dementia involves cognitive difficulties severe enough to disrupt daily life. Identifying lifestyle habits associated with lower dementia risk is therefore an important area of research, particularly as populations grow older. The findings suggest that regular caffeinated coffee consumption may be one such habit. However, the results show an association rather than proving that coffee directly prevents dementia. Other differences between coffee drinkers and people who avoid coffee could also contribute to the observed results. The potential benefits were not limited to diagnosed dementia. Participants who drank more caffeinated coffee were also less likely to report that their memory or thinking abilities had declined. Researchers found that 7.8% of adults who consumed higher amounts of caffeinated coffee reported subjective cognitive decline, compared with 9.5% of those who rarely or never drank it. Subjective cognitive decline refers to changes in memory or thinking that people notice themselves, even when those difficulties have not necessarily been confirmed by formal cognitive testing. Someone experiencing it might feel that remembering information, concentrating, or finding the right words has become more difficult. Such complaints do not automatically indicate dementia. Nevertheless, they can provide useful information about how people perceive changes in their cognitive abilities as they grow older. The lower percentage among caffeinated coffee drinkers adds to the evidence linking coffee consumption with healthier cognitive aging. The researchers also examined whether the amount of coffee consumed was related to the strength of the observed benefits. Drinking two to three cups of caffeinated coffee per day was associated with the most favorable outcomes for dementia risk and cognitive functioning. Notably, this association remained apparent regardless of participants' genetic risk of developing dementia. In other words, the relationship between coffee consumption and brain health was observed even among people whose inherited characteristics might make them more vulnerable to the disease. Genetic risk refers to the influence of inherited variations in DNA that can increase or decrease a person's likelihood of developing certain conditions. Although genetics can play an important role in dementia, they are only one part of a much larger picture that includes age, general health, and lifestyle. The results also suggest that drinking larger amounts of coffee is not necessarily better. Consumption beyond the range associated with the strongest benefits did not appear to provide additional protection. Coffee was not the only beverage associated with better brain health. Researchers found that drinking tea was also linked to lower dementia risk and better cognitive functioning. For tea, the strongest associations appeared among participants who consumed one to two cups per day. As with coffee, drinking more than this amount did not appear to produce further benefits. However, the study did not distinguish between caffeinated and noncaffeinated tea. As a result, the findings cannot establish whether caffeine was responsible for the association observed among tea drinkers. The results for coffee offered an additional clue. While regular caffeinated coffee was associated with lower dementia risk and better cognitive outcomes, decaffeinated coffee did not demonstrate the same benefits. Caffeine is a naturally occurring stimulant found in coffee, tea, and several other plants. It acts on the central nervous system and is best known for temporarily increasing alertness and reducing feelings of tiredness. Whether caffeine also contributes to better brain health over many years is a separate question. The difference between regular and decaffeinated coffee makes this possibility worth investigating, but it does not establish caffeine as the cause of the observed benefits. Taken together, the findings suggest that moderate consumption of caffeinated coffee and tea may be associated with healthier brain aging. For coffee drinkers, two to three cups daily appeared to offer the strongest association, while one to two cups of tea showed the most favorable results among tea drinkers. Although additional research is needed to determine whether these beverages directly influence dementia risk, the long-term findings offer encouraging news for people who already enjoy coffee or tea as part of their daily routine.
